finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto the authenticated user object and persists it. Any authenticated user can set privileged fields such as role, isAdmin, id, email or tenant/org, giving privilege escalation or account takeover. The full user object is also returned in the response.
finding.source: req.body JSON of an authenticated PUT /me request, with attacker-chosen keys (e.g. {"role":"admin"}, {"isAdmin":true})

trace.note: Handler for PUT /me receives the request
Object.assign merges all attacker-supplied keys into req.user with no allowlist
The modified user is persisted via req.store.save
The full user object is returned in the response

finding.guards_checked: No field allowlist, schema validation, or role/ownership check in this file. The authentication middleware that sets req.user is not in the directory, so it was not reviewed. Even if it exists, it would not restrict which fields are written. The sibling /me/profile route (line 11) shows the intended allowlist of displayName and bio, which is missing here.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation and users.js:6 persists it, while the sibling route at users.js:11-12 shows the allowlist this route lacks; the auth middleware that sets req.user is not in the directory, but an authenticated low-privilege user can still write arbitrary fields.

verdict_facts.reason: users.js:5 runs Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist, users.js:6 persists it and users.js:7 returns it, so any authenticated user can set fields like role; the /me/profile route at users.js:11-12 shows the intended allowlist that /me lacks.
